headline: Cape Town Erupts Over Baboon Deportation; Deportees Seen Boarding Van Voluntarily
subheadline: *The 44-member Waterfall troop is being moved to a luxury wildlife sanctuary, sparking history's first protest in which the deportees appeared to be enjoying the snacks.*
author: Thandi Mokoena, Primate Affairs Desk
seoTitle: Cape Town Baboon 'Deportation' Sparks Human Blockade
seoDescription: Satire: Cape Town residents formed human blockades to stop 44 baboons being relocated to a luxury sanctuary. The deportees reportedly climbed in voluntarily.
sourceEvent: The 44-member Waterfall baboon troop was captured in the Cape Town suburb of Simon's Town and is being relocated to a wildlife sanctuary, a move officials say is needed to end human-wildlife conflict. Local residents protested and attempted to block the transport vehicle, and a second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

social.x: Cape Town residents formed a human blockade to stop 44 baboons being relocated to a luxury sanctuary — believed to be the first deportation protest where the deportees climbed into the van voluntarily and looked thrilled about it.
social.facebook: Residents of Simon's Town linked arms this weekend to block the relocation of the 44-member Waterfall baboon troop to a wildlife sanctuary featuring shaded climbing structures, natural rock pools and a daily feeding schedule described as 'better than most airlines.' The protest is believed to be the first deportation demonstration in history where the deportees entered the vehicle voluntarily, appeared to be enjoying snacks, and passed fruit back to the crowd 'as though offering condolences.' A second troop is due to be moved next, and several neighbours have reportedly begun leaving out fruit to speed things along.
social.linkedin: The Cape Town baboon relocation raises an underexplored stakeholder-engagement question: what happens when the affected parties register no objection and the objectors are, by every observable metric, third parties? A case study in consultation asymmetry below.

altHeadlines: Residents Rage as Baboons Relocated to Facility With Better Amenities Than Most Flats
Baboon Troop Deported to Luxury Sanctuary; Locals Demand Same Deal

body:
CAPE TOWN — Residents of the seaside suburb of Simon's Town formed human blockades this weekend in an attempt to stop the relocation of a 44-member baboon troop to a luxury wildlife sanctuary, in what experts believe is the first deportation protest in recorded history where the deportees were seen voluntarily climbing into the van.

The Waterfall troop — so named after the area it mainly inhabits, and not, as one placard claimed, 'because property values there have gone off a cliff' — was captured Friday and Saturday after years of escalating conflict with humans, including home invasions, car break-ins and one incident in which a baboon reportedly ate a tourist's entire packed lunch 'while maintaining sustained eye contact.'

Officials insist the move is necessary to protect both primates and people. Locals counter that the baboons are being deported to a facility that sounds, on balance, nicer than their own homes. 'It has acacia trees, a dedicated enrichment programme and a vet on call twenty-four hours a day,' said local man Pieter Erasmus, 52, who has been on a waiting list for a doctor's appointment since March. 'I would like to be relocated, please.'

Tensions peaked Saturday when a crowd linked arms in front of the transport vehicle, chanting 'HADEDAS STAY, BABOONS STAY' — a reference to the hadeda ibis, a local bird so widely despised that no resident could explain why it had been included — and 'WHOSE STREETS? THEIR STREETS.'

The demonstration reportedly faltered when the baboons, who had entered the van of their own accord after following a trail of fruit, began passing objects back to protesters through the mesh 'as though offering condolences.'

'It was humiliating,' said one demonstrator, who asked not to be named because she had accepted a grape from a deportee. 'We came to save them. One of them patted the floor of the van like, hop in, it's lovely in here.'

A municipal spokesperson stressed the sanctuary is 'not a resort,' before confirming it offers shaded climbing structures, natural rock pools and a feeding schedule 'better than most airlines.' Asked whether the baboons had been consulted, the spokesperson said the troop had expressed a clear preference 'in the sense that they kept choosing to stand on the fruit.'

A second, smaller troop from nearby Seaforth is due to be moved next, a prospect that has split the community into two camps: residents opposed to the relocation, and residents who have begun leaving fruit on their doorsteps in the hope of accelerating it. 'My neighbour put out a fruit bowl,' said one local woman. 'For herself? No. She's bribing them with papaya.'

Wildlife analysts note the standoff is a rare inversion of the usual human-wildlife conflict. 'Typically the animals want to stay and the humans want them gone,' said one analyst. 'Here the animals appear to want to go, the humans want them to stay, and the fruit wants nothing to do with any of it.'

The municipality confirmed the Waterfall troop is settling in well, describing its members as 'relaxed, curious, and already better behaved than the residents' association WhatsApp group.'

At press time, three protesters had been turned away from the sanctuary gates after attempting to claim asylum as baboons.
